notes:
1. Structure of an Economy — Meaning

  • The structure of an economy refers to the distribution of production, employment, income, ownership, institutions and economic activities across different sectors.
  • India's economy is highly diversified and includes agriculture, manufacturing, construction, trade, transport, finance, technology and public services.

2. Main Ways to Classify the Indian Economy

Economic activity can be classified by:

  • Sector → Primary, Secondary, Tertiary.
  • Ownership → Public, Private, Cooperative.
  • Employment → Organised, Unorganised, Formal, Informal.
  • Location → Rural, Urban.
  • Economic linkage → Domestic and External sectors.

3. Three-Sector Classification

  • Primary sector → Direct use or extraction of natural resources.
  • Secondary sector → Manufacturing, construction and related production.
  • Tertiary sector → Services.
📌 Must-Memorise

Primary → Natural Resources

Secondary → Production / Construction

Tertiary → Services

4. Primary Sector — Main Activities

The primary sector includes:

  • Agriculture.
  • Animal husbandry.
  • Forestry.
  • Fishing.
  • Mining.
  • Quarrying.
📌 Must-Memorise

Primary Sector → Agriculture + Allied Activities + Mining

5. Secondary Sector — Main Activities

The secondary sector includes:

  • Manufacturing.
  • Construction.
  • Electricity.
  • Gas.
  • Water supply.
  • Related industrial production.

6. Tertiary Sector — Main Activities

The tertiary sector includes:

  • Trade.
  • Hotels.
  • Transport.
  • Storage.
  • Communication.
  • Banking.
  • Insurance.
  • Real estate.
  • Information technology.
  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Professional services.
  • Public administration.

7. Sectoral Interdependence

  • Primary, secondary and tertiary sectors are strongly interconnected.
  • Agriculture supplies food and raw materials.
  • Industry supplies machinery, fertilisers and manufactured inputs.
  • Services provide finance, transport, insurance, trade and communication.
📌 Must-Memorise

Agriculture → Raw Materials

Industry → Machinery and Inputs

Services → Finance + Transport + Trade

8. Agriculture — Structural Importance

Agriculture remains important because it provides:

  • Food.
  • Employment.
  • Rural income.
  • Raw materials for industry.
  • Demand for industrial goods.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Lower GDP Share ≠ Agriculture Is Unimportant

9. Agro-Based Industrial Linkages

Agriculture supports industries such as:

  • Textiles.
  • Sugar.
  • Food processing.
  • Edible oils.
  • Dairy.
  • Leather-related activities.

10. Agriculture — Demand Linkage with Industry

Agriculture creates demand for:

  • Tractors.
  • Pumps.
  • Fertilisers.
  • Machinery.
  • Consumer goods.

11. Agricultural Employment-Output Imbalance

  • Agriculture employs a much larger share of workers than its relative contribution to output.
  • This creates a major structural imbalance in the Indian economy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Agriculture → High Employment Share + Lower Output Share

12. Labour Productivity in Agriculture

  • When many workers generate a relatively smaller share of output, average labour productivity tends to be lower.
  • Raising agricultural productivity is therefore important for structural transformation.

13. Structural Transformation — Agriculture Dimension

India requires:

  • Higher agricultural productivity.
  • Greater productive employment outside agriculture.

14. Allied Agricultural Activities

Important allied activities include:

  • Animal husbandry.
  • Dairy.
  • Fisheries.
  • Forestry.
  • Horticulture.

These contribute to:

  • Rural income.
  • Nutrition.
  • Employment.
  • Exports.
  • Diversification.

15. Horticulture — Main Components

Horticulture includes:

  • Fruits.
  • Vegetables.
  • Flowers.
  • Spices.
  • Plantation crops.

16. Agricultural Diversification

  • Diversification into dairy, livestock, fisheries and horticulture can reduce excessive dependence on crop farming.
  • It can also create more stable and varied rural income sources.

17. Industrialisation — Meaning and Importance

  • Industrialisation means expansion of manufacturing, construction and related productive activities.
  • It can raise productivity, create non-farm employment, support urbanisation and strengthen exports.

18. Major Manufacturing Activities in India

Important industrial activities include:

  • Automobiles and auto components.
  • Pharmaceuticals.
  • Chemicals.
  • Textiles and garments.
  • Iron and steel.
  • Cement.
  • Engineering industries.
  • Electronics.
  • Electrical equipment.
  • Food processing.

19. Manufacturing — Structural Role

Manufacturing:

  • Converts inputs into higher-value products.
  • Creates value addition.
  • Can absorb workers moving out of agriculture.
  • Supports exports.
  • Can reduce dependence on imports in relevant sectors.

20. Construction — Secondary Sector

  • Construction is part of the secondary sector.
  • It includes residential buildings, commercial buildings, roads, bridges, industrial facilities and infrastructure.
  • It is also an important source of labour-intensive employment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Construction → Secondary Sector

21. Services — Largest Output Contributor

  • The services sector has become the largest contributor to India's national output.
  • Rapid expansion of services is one of the most distinctive features of India's economic structure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Largest Output Sector → Services

22. Modern Services

Modern services include:

  • Information technology.
  • Telecommunications.
  • Finance.
  • Digital services.
  • Professional services.
  • Business-process services.

23. Traditional Services

Traditional services include:

  • Retail trade.
  • Transport.
  • Repair services.
  • Small hospitality establishments.
  • Personal services.
  • Productivity and income vary widely within these activities.

24. India and Technology-Enabled Services

  • India has developed a strong international position in information technology and technology-enabled services.
  • Services exports have become an important part of India's external economic strength.

25. Output and Employment — Sectoral Divergence

  • Sectoral shares in output and employment are not identical.
  • Agriculture has high employment but lower output share.
  • Services have a much higher output share.
  • Industry occupies an important intermediate position.

26. Structural Transformation — Meaning

  • Structural transformation is the long-term movement of economic activity from lower-productivity activities towards higher-productivity activities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Structural Transformation → Movement Toward Higher Productivity

27. Typical Structural Transformation Pattern

A developing economy often experiences:

  • Agriculture's share of output ↓.
  • Agriculture's share of employment ↓.
  • Industry ↑.
  • Services ↑.
  • Productivity ↑.

28. India's Distinctive Structural Pattern

  • India's agricultural output share declined significantly.
  • Services expanded rapidly.
  • Manufacturing did not absorb labour on the same scale seen in some East Asian economies.
📌 Must-Memorise

India → Service-Led Structural Transformation

29. Lewis-Type Development Idea

  • Development economics commonly describes transformation as movement of labour from traditional low-productivity activities to modern higher-productivity activities.
  • India's challenge is to make this movement productive rather than merely shifting workers geographically.

30. Organised Sector — Meaning

  • The organised sector broadly consists of enterprises operating within formal regulatory and institutional frameworks.

Such establishments are more likely to:

  • Maintain formal accounts.
  • Follow tax laws.
  • Follow labour laws.
  • Provide structured employment conditions.

31. Organised-Sector Examples

Examples include:

  • Government departments.
  • Public-sector enterprises.
  • Banks.
  • Registered companies.
  • Large establishments.

32. Unorganised Sector — Meaning

  • The unorganised sector largely consists of small enterprises and workers with limited registration, regulation or social-security coverage.

Examples include:

  • Street vendors.
  • Domestic workers.
  • Small traders.
  • Agricultural labourers.
  • Casual construction workers.
  • Workers in very small enterprises.

33. Formal Employment

Formal employment generally involves:

  • Recognised employer-employee relationship.
  • Regular employment records.
  • Defined wages.
  • Greater legal protection.
  • Greater social-security access.

34. Informal Employment

Informal employment often involves:

  • Insecure work arrangements.
  • Irregular income.
  • Limited social protection.
  • Absence of written contracts.
  • Weak bargaining power.

35. Organised Sector vs Formal Employment

  • Organised sector and formal employment are related but not identical.
  • A formally registered enterprise can still employ workers under informal arrangements.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Organised Sector ≠ Always Formal Employment

36. Informal Economy — Main Problems

Informal workers and enterprises may face:

  • Income instability.
  • Limited social security.
  • Lack of paid leave.
  • Weak bargaining power.
  • Limited formal credit access.

37. Formalisation — Development Objective

  • Formalisation of enterprises and workers can improve record-keeping, social protection, access to finance and regulatory compliance.
  • It is therefore an important long-term development objective.

38. Public Sector — Meaning and Role

  • Public-sector activities are owned or controlled by government.

Historically important areas include:

  • Infrastructure.
  • Energy.
  • Defence production.
  • Transport.
  • Banking.
  • Heavy industry.
  • Strategic sectors.

39. Public Enterprises — Developmental Role

  • Public enterprises may pursue developmental and social objectives in addition to commercial objectives.
  • Their role can therefore extend beyond profit maximisation.

40. Private Sector — Meaning and Role

  • The private sector consists of businesses owned by individuals, partnerships, companies and other non-government entities.
  • It plays a major role in manufacturing, services, construction, trade, technology, finance and investment.

41. Economic Reforms and Private-Sector Expansion

  • Economic reforms beginning in 1991 increased the role of private-sector participation in many economic activities.

42. Cooperative Sector

  • Cooperative enterprises are collectively owned by members sharing common economic interests.

Important areas include:

  • Dairy.
  • Agricultural credit.
  • Marketing.
  • Housing.
  • Consumer services.

43. Cooperative Ownership — Core Distinction

  • Public → Government-owned or controlled.
  • Private → Non-government ownership.
  • Cooperative → Member-owned.
📌 Must-Memorise

Public → Government

Private → Non-Government

Cooperative → Members

44. Public Ownership vs Regulation

  • Government regulation does not automatically convert a private enterprise into a public-sector enterprise.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Regulated Private Company ≠ Public-Sector Enterprise

45. Rural Economy — Beyond Agriculture

  • The rural economy is closely linked with agriculture but is not limited to farming.

Rural non-farm activities include:

  • Construction.
  • Manufacturing.
  • Transport.
  • Retail.
  • Services.

46. Rural Diversification

  • Expansion of non-farm rural employment reduces excessive dependence on agriculture.
  • It can raise household resilience and broaden rural income sources.

47. Urban Economy

Urban economic activity contains larger concentrations of:

  • Manufacturing.
  • Construction.
  • Banking.
  • Trade.
  • IT.
  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Transport.
  • Administration.

48. Urbanisation — Meaning and Benefits

  • Urbanisation means increasing concentration of population and economic activity in towns and cities.
  • Urban areas can improve productivity through better infrastructure, markets, transport and knowledge networks.

49. Urbanisation — Major Pressures

Rapid urbanisation can create:

  • Housing shortages.
  • Traffic congestion.
  • Pollution.
  • Water stress.
  • Sanitation pressure.
  • Informal settlements.

50. Balanced Urban Development

  • Sustainable urbanisation requires planning, infrastructure, housing and effective public services.
  • Urban growth without adequate infrastructure can reduce productivity and quality of life.

51. MSME — Meaning

  • MSME stands for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises.
  • MSMEs operate in both manufacturing and services.
📌 Must-Memorise

MSME → Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises

52. MSMEs — Economic Role

MSMEs contribute to:

  • Employment.
  • Entrepreneurship.
  • Exports.
  • Regional development.
  • Supply chains.
  • Linkages between small and large firms.

53. MSME Constraints

Major constraints include:

  • Limited formal credit.
  • Delayed payments.
  • Technology gaps.
  • Weak market access.
  • Infrastructure problems.
  • Relatively high compliance burden.

54. MSME Strengthening

MSMEs can be strengthened through:

  • Better credit access.
  • Technology adoption.
  • Digitalisation.
  • Better market access.
  • Improved infrastructure.

55. Infrastructure — Foundation of Economic Activity

  • Infrastructure supports productive economic activity and human development.
  • Weak infrastructure raises costs and can discourage investment.

56. Economic vs Social Infrastructure

Economic infrastructure includes:

  • Transport.
  • Electricity.
  • Communication.
  • Irrigation.
  • Logistics.
  • Digital networks.

Social infrastructure includes:

  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Sanitation.
  • Housing.
📌 Must-Memorise

Economic Infrastructure → Production Support

Social Infrastructure → Human Development

57. Core Industries — Basic Inputs

Important core inputs include:

  • Electricity.
  • Steel.
  • Cement.
  • Coal.
  • Petroleum-related products.
  • These support agriculture, manufacturing, construction and services.

58. Infrastructure and Competitiveness

  • Better transport, power and logistics reduce production and transaction costs.
  • Strong infrastructure can attract investment and improve competitiveness.

59. Logistics — Meaning

  • Logistics concerns the movement, storage and coordination of goods.

Important logistics infrastructure includes:

  • Roads.
  • Railways.
  • Ports.
  • Airports.
  • Warehousing.
  • Digital tracking systems.

60. Efficient Logistics — Benefit

  • Efficient logistics reduces transport time and cost.
  • It also strengthens supply chains and export competitiveness.

61. Digital Infrastructure

Digital infrastructure includes:

  • Communication networks.
  • Data systems.
  • Digital payments.
  • Digital identity.
  • Online public-service systems.

It can improve:

  • Market access.
  • Financial inclusion.
  • Government efficiency.

62. Savings — Economic Role

  • Savings provide financial resources that can be channelled into investment.
  • Savings can originate from households, businesses and the public sector.

63. Investment and Capital Formation

  • Investment creates productive assets.
  • Capital formation means creation of productive assets that can raise future output.
📌 Must-Memorise

Capital Formation → Creation of Productive Assets

64. Capital Formation — Examples

Capital formation includes:

  • Factories.
  • Machinery.
  • Roads.
  • Irrigation facilities.
  • Power plants.
  • Productive infrastructure.

65. Savings-Investment Chain

Savings

→ Financial Intermediation

→ Investment

→ Productive Assets

→ Future Output

📌 Must-Memorise

Savings → Investment → Capital Formation → Growth

66. Financial Intermediation

Institutions channeling savings into investment include:

  • Banks.
  • Capital markets.
  • Insurance companies.
  • Other financial institutions.

67. Gross Capital Formation

  • Gross capital formation broadly refers to additions to fixed assets and inventories in the economy.
  • Higher productive capital formation can support long-term growth.

68. Investment Quality

  • The quality of investment is as important as the quantity.
  • Poorly planned investment can create assets with weak economic or social returns.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

More Investment ≠ Automatically Productive Investment

69. External Sector — Meaning

  • The external sector connects India's domestic economy with the global economy through trade, investment, finance, technology, remittances and services.

70. Exports and Imports

Exports:

  • Create foreign demand for Indian goods and services.

Imports can provide:

  • Energy.
  • Raw materials.
  • Machinery.
  • Technology.
  • Consumer goods.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Imports ≠ Only Consumption

71. FDI — Foreign Direct Investment

FDI can provide:

  • Capital.
  • Technology.
  • Managerial expertise.
  • Access to global production networks.

72. FPI — Foreign Portfolio Investment

  • FPI provides financial capital through portfolio assets.
  • It can be more volatile than direct investment.
📌 Must-Memorise

FDI → Productive / Long-Term Presence

FPI → Financial Portfolio Capital

73. Services Exports and Remittances

  • India has strong capabilities in IT and business-service exports.
  • Remittances from Indians working abroad contribute to household income and foreign-exchange receipts.

74. Global Value Chains

  • Global value chains divide different stages of production across countries.
  • A product may be designed, manufactured in parts and assembled in different countries.

Participation can support:

  • Manufacturing.
  • Exports.
  • Technology transfer.
  • Integration with global markets.

75. Structural Imbalances in India

Major imbalances include:

  • Agriculture → High employment relative to output.
  • Informal sector → Large employment presence.
  • Regional disparities → Unequal development.
  • Productivity → Significant differences across sectors.

76. Regional Disparities

States differ in:

  • Infrastructure.
  • Human development.
  • Urbanisation.
  • Investment.
  • Per capita income.
  • Economic structure.

77. Balanced Regional Development

Balanced regional development requires improvements in:

  • Infrastructure.
  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Connectivity.
  • Investment.
  • Administrative capacity.

78. Fiscal Transfers and Regional Development

  • Union fiscal transfers can support States with weaker revenue capacity.
  • Transfers alone are insufficient without effective governance, human capital and local institutional capacity.

79. Productivity and Worker Movement

  • Productivity differences contribute to wage and income differences between sectors.
  • Movement of labour into higher-productivity activities can raise average incomes.

80. Conditions for Productive Labour Movement

Structural transformation requires:

  • Skills.
  • Labour mobility.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Job creation.

81. Digitalisation — Structural Change

Digitalisation is transforming:

  • Banking.
  • Payments.
  • Retail.
  • Communication.
  • Government services.
  • Business models.

82. Automation and Artificial Intelligence

  • Automation changes production processes and labour requirements.
  • Artificial intelligence is changing skill requirements, business models and productivity possibilities.

83. Renewable Energy and Electric Mobility

  • Renewable energy is changing investment patterns and the energy structure.
  • Electric mobility is influencing automobile production, energy demand and infrastructure investment.

84. E-Commerce and Fintech

  • E-commerce is transforming retail and logistics.
  • Financial technology is expanding digital payments and financial-service access.

85. Platform and Gig Economy

  • Platform-based businesses create new forms of service delivery and employment.
  • Gig work includes short-term, task-based or platform-mediated work.

Examples include:

  • App-based transport.
  • Delivery services.
  • Freelance digital work.

86. Gig Economy — Advantage and Challenge

Advantage:

  • Greater flexibility for workers and firms.

Challenge:

  • Income insecurity.
  • Limited social protection.

87. Green Economy

Green-economy activities include:

  • Renewable energy.
  • Electric mobility.
  • Energy efficiency.
  • Waste management.
  • Sustainable infrastructure.

88. Knowledge Economy

  • A knowledge economy relies heavily on skills, technology, research, innovation and information.

Important Indian knowledge sectors include:

  • Information technology.
  • Pharmaceuticals.
  • Biotechnology.
  • Engineering.
  • Digital services.

89. Sectoral Memory Chain

  • Primary → Natural resources.
  • Secondary → Manufacturing + Construction.
  • Tertiary → Services.
  • Agriculture → High employment.
  • Services → Largest output contributor.

90. Structural Transformation Memory Chain

Agriculture Output Share ↓

→ Industry and Services ↑

→ Productivity ↑

India's distinctive pattern:

Services ↑ rapidly

Manufacturing labour absorption → Relatively limited

91. Formal-Informal Memory Chain

  • Organised enterprise ≠ Always formal employment.
  • Informal work can exist inside organised firms.
  • Formalisation → Records + Protection + Compliance + Finance.

92. Ownership Memory Chain

  • Public → Government.
  • Private → Individuals / Companies.
  • Cooperative → Members.

93. Rural-Urban Memory Chain

  • Rural → Agriculture + Non-Farm Activities.
  • Urban → Manufacturing + Services + Administration.
  • Urbanisation → Productivity Gains + Infrastructure Pressure.

94. MSME Memory Chain

MSME

→ Employment

→ Entrepreneurship

→ Exports

→ Supply Chains

→ Regional Development

95. Infrastructure Memory Chain

  • Economic → Transport + Power + Communication + Irrigation.
  • Social → Education + Health + Sanitation + Housing.
  • Digital → Networks + Payments + Identity + Public Services.

96. Savings and Investment Memory Chain

Savings

→ Investment

→ Capital Formation

→ Productive Capacity

→ Growth

97. External Sector Memory Chain

Exports

  • Imports
  • FDI
  • FPI
  • Services
  • Remittances
  • Global Value Chains

98. Emerging Economy Memory Chain

Digitalisation

→ AI

→ Automation

→ Renewable Energy

→ E-Commerce

→ Fintech

→ Gig Economy

99. TNPSC Traps

  • Agriculture belongs to the primary sector.
  • Animal husbandry belongs to the primary sector.
  • Fisheries belong to the primary sector.
  • Forestry belongs to the primary sector.
  • Mining and quarrying belong to the primary sector.
  • Manufacturing belongs to the secondary sector.
  • Construction belongs to the secondary sector.
  • Banking belongs to the tertiary sector.
  • IT belongs to the tertiary sector.
  • Education and health are services.
  • Services are the largest contributor to India's output.
  • Agriculture remains structurally important despite lower output share.
  • Agriculture employs a larger share of workers relative to its output.
  • Structural transformation does not mean disappearance of agriculture.
  • India has experienced rapid service-led transformation.
  • Manufacturing labour absorption has been relatively limited.
  • Organised sector and formal employment are not identical.
  • Informal employment can exist inside organised firms.
  • Government regulation does not make a private firm public-sector.
  • Rural economy is not limited to farming.
  • Construction is a secondary-sector activity.
  • Cooperatives are member-owned.
  • MSMEs operate in manufacturing and services.
  • Economic and social infrastructure are different.
  • Transport and electricity are economic infrastructure.
  • Education and health are social infrastructure.
  • Capital formation means creation of productive assets.
  • Capital formation does not mean merely holding money.
  • Savings provide resources for investment.
  • Investment quality matters as much as quantity.
  • Imports can support production through energy, machinery, technology and raw materials.
  • Services can be exported.
  • FDI and FPI are different.
  • FPI can be relatively more volatile.
  • Remittances contribute to household income and foreign-exchange receipts.
  • Regional disparities can persist despite national growth.
  • Digitalisation is changing economic structure.
  • Gig work provides flexibility but can create social-protection concerns.
  • Green economy involves sustainable economic activities.
  • Knowledge economy depends heavily on skills, technology and innovation.

100. Ultra-Short Memory Chain

  • Primary → Natural Resources.
  • Secondary → Manufacturing + Construction.
  • Tertiary → Services.
  • Agriculture → High Employment.
  • Services → Largest Output Share.
  • Transformation → Higher Productivity.
  • Organised ≠ Formal.
  • Public → Government.
  • Private → Non-Government.
  • Cooperative → Members.
  • Rural ≠ Farming Only.
  • MSME → Jobs + Exports.
  • Economic Infrastructure → Production.
  • Social Infrastructure → Human Development.
  • Savings → Investment.
  • Investment → Capital Formation.
  • Exports → Foreign Demand.
  • Imports → Inputs + Technology.
  • FDI → Productive Capital.
  • FPI → Financial Capital.
  • Gig → Task-Based Work.
  • Green → Sustainable Activities.
  • Knowledge → Skills + Technology.

101. Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

  • Structure of economy means? → Distribution of production, employment, income, ownership, institutions and activities.
  • Three main sectors? → Primary, secondary and tertiary.
  • Agriculture belongs to? → Primary sector.
  • Forestry? → Primary sector.
  • Fisheries? → Primary sector.
  • Mining? → Primary sector.
  • Manufacturing? → Secondary sector.
  • Construction? → Secondary sector.
  • Banking? → Tertiary sector.
  • IT? → Tertiary sector.
  • Largest contributor to India's output? → Services sector.
  • Why is agriculture important? → Food, employment, rural income and industrial linkages.
  • Main agricultural structural challenge? → High employment share relative to output.
  • Structural transformation means? → Movement towards higher-productivity activities.
  • India's distinctive structural pattern? → Rapid services expansion with relatively limited manufacturing labour absorption.
  • Organised sector means? → Enterprises operating within formal regulatory structures.
  • Informal employment means? → Work with limited security, records or social protection.
  • Organised sector and formal employment identical? → No.
  • Public sector means? → Government-owned or controlled.
  • Private sector means? → Non-government ownership.
  • Cooperative sector means? → Member-owned enterprise.
  • Rural economy limited to farming? → No.
  • Urbanisation means? → Increasing concentration of population and economic activity in towns and cities.
  • Main urban pressures? → Housing, congestion, pollution, water and sanitation.
  • MSME full form? → Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises.
  • MSMEs operate in? → Manufacturing and services.
  • Major MSME roles? → Employment, entrepreneurship, exports and regional development.
  • Economic infrastructure examples? → Transport, power, communication, irrigation and logistics.
  • Social infrastructure examples? → Education, health, sanitation and housing.
  • Capital formation means? → Creation of productive assets.
  • Savings support? → Investment.
  • Investment creates? → Productive assets.
  • Gross capital formation broadly represents? → Additions to fixed assets and inventories.
  • Exports do what? → Create foreign demand.
  • Imports can provide? → Energy, raw materials, machinery and technology.
  • FDI can provide? → Capital, technology and managerial expertise.
  • FPI characteristic? → Financial capital that can be relatively volatile.
  • Remittances provide? → Household income and foreign-exchange receipts.
  • Global value chains mean? → Production stages distributed across countries.
  • Main regional structural challenge? → Unequal income, infrastructure, productivity and development across States.
  • Digitalisation affects? → Banking, payments, retail, communication and government services.
  • Gig economy means? → Short-term, task-based or platform-mediated work.
  • Green economy includes? → Renewable energy, electric mobility, efficiency and sustainable infrastructure.
  • Knowledge economy depends on? → Skills, technology, innovation, research and information.
  • Core Indian structural chain? → Agriculture Employment-Intensive → Services Output-Dominant → Industry Crucial for Productive Transformation.
